title: Democrats hope a familiar name can help put Indiana back in play | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Democrats are dreaming of building on their midterm gains across Middle America — and in Indiana, a scion of the state’s most famous political family is igniting the party’s hopes that the Rust Belt’s reddest state might soon be in play.

Beau Bayh, the 31-year-old grandson of Sen. Birch Bayh and son of Evan Bayh, the former governor and senator, didn’t just win the Indiana secretary of state’s race in his first run for political office. He was perhaps the party’s single strongest performer nationwide: He improved by 28 percentage points on President Donald Trump’s 2024 margin in the state on his way to a 9-point win — the biggest swing in the continental United States.

Bayh led a Democratic ticket that saw stunning success. The party flipped a congressional seat; ousted the state House speaker and broke the GOP’s supermajority in the chamber; and won the state comptroller’s office for the first time since the 1980s. It’s giving some hope to Democrats, who haven’t held the governor’s mansion for two decades and have carried the state in only one presidential election — 2008 — in six decades.

“It’s just a thrilling result,” said Pete Buttigieg, the likely2028 Democratic presidential candidatewhose own political career began with a loss in the race for Indiana state treasurer in 2010. He campaigned alongside Bayh, and said the race was one that showed “candidate quality really mattered.”

“This is part of why I always insist that there’s no such thing as a permanently red state or seat,” he said. “I think the real question now is: When you have something that defies the pattern, is that a blip or is that the beginning of a new pattern? And that all depends on what we do next.”

The governor’s office and a Senate seat will also be on the ballot in 2028. And the chatter about Bayh potentially following the same path as his father, who was elected governor two years after being elected secretary of state, was already underway long before election night.

“I think he could most definitely be a future governor,” said Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the Democratic Governors Association chairman who has hosted Bayh on his podcast twice.

There were plenty of signs even before Election Day that Republicans see in Bayh a likely future challenger. His run received an unusual amount of national attention.

Vice President JD Vance said Bayh is “a Trojan horse for radical Democrats to destroy election integrity and launch a takeover of Indiana.” Donald Trump Jr. called Bayh “just another leftist radical cosplaying as a moderate.” Sen. Jim Banks, who helped engineer Republican Max Engling’s nomination to take on Bayh, said Bayh “is a liberal, not a moderate.”

The prospect of competition from a Democrat for the first time in years “frightened them, and perhaps it should,” Evan Bayh told CNN.

“The political establishment in Indiana for too long hadn’t had to work for anything,” he said. “They’re afraid of him because they know that he may be the only one who can hold the political class in Indiana accountable and create real competition in our politics.”

Expectations about Bayh’s political future are “very high, and they should be,” said state Rep. Ed Delaney, an Indianapolis Democrat and friend of the Bayhs who has known Beau and his twin brother, Nick, since they were children.

He said many Democrats believe first-term Republican Gov. Mike Braun will be vulnerable as he seeks a second term in 2028 — and could potentially even lose his party’s nomination, as state Attorney General Todd Rokita positions himself take Braun on in the primary.

“We want to be led out of the desert to some extent, and he’s capable of that,” Delaney said of Bayh.

One veteran Indiana Republican strategist said members of the Bayh family have “a history of opportunism” when it comes to running for office against weak GOP nominees.

But, the strategist added: “Indiana Republicans need to get our own house in order before we start worrying about who’s on the Democrat ticket.”

Democratic influence across the Midwest had waned during President Trump’s era in part because of his dominance in smaller towns and rural areas, where winning small populations by massive margins added up to leads Democrats couldn’t match with support from urban and suburban voters.

But that changed this year, asDemocrats picked up supportin rural as well as suburban and urban communities en route to winning key races in several Midwestern states. (The same phenomenon also helped the party scorehistoric victories in the South.)

In Indiana, Bayh’s biggest gain came in rural Perry County along the Ohio River. Trump won the county by 30 points in 2025; Bayh won it by 9 points.

Another huge swing came in Vigo County, home of Terre Haute — Birch Bayh’s hometown. Until recently, the county was famous forbeing a bellwetherin presidential elections. Trump won it by 18 points in 2024; Bayh won it by 18 points this year.

“The harsh reality is, people are frustrated. They are looking for a next generation of leadership that’s not necessarily progressive or MAGA,” said Terre Haute Mayor Brandon Sakbun, who at 30 is widely seen as another rising Democratic star, and who chaired Bayh’s campaign.

Similar swings occurred across much of southern Indiana, a region that is vital to Democrats’ success in the state.

It was that region’s willingness to elect not just members of the Bayh family, but moderate and conservative Democrats to the state legislature, that set up Indiana’s last epic era of political battles. Hard-charging Republican Gov. Mitch Daniels and his nemesis, Democrat Pat Bauer, an old-school operator who was state House speaker, brawled over labor rights, education reforms, property taxes and more — and the outcomes of those fights in many ways define the state today.

By 2014, those same ancestral Democratic voters had swung hard in the GOP’s favor and ended Indiana’s status as a political battleground. Then the Trump era all but wiped out the Democratic Party in the state.

Bayh said part of why Democrats had lost their connection to those rural areas is that party members lapsing into academia-speak has been “breaking some cultural relationship between you and the voters.”

He said Democrats need to spend more time “talking to people like a normal person.”

Bayh, a 6-foot-3 former Marine who lifted weights in campaign ads, launched his campaign with a message of taking on corruption he said was festering at the statehouse after 16 years of one-party rule.

It made sense at the time: The Republican secretary of state, Diego Morales, faced a long list of ethics controversies — including scrutiny over no-bid contracts, hiring his brother-in-law for a six-figure state government job and the purchase of a $90,000 vehicle with state dollars. Morales has consistently denied wrongdoing.

But Bayh’s campaign faced a difficult choice in June, when Morales dropped out of the race just before the state GOP convention. There, the party nominated Engling, a longtime Capitol Hill staffer who worked for Indiana Republican Sen. Jim Banks. It was a choice intended to cleanse the party’s ticket of any stench of controversy and neutralize Bayh’s corruption attacks.

Bayh stuck with it, describing Morales as “a symptom of a larger problem.” He made taking on corruption the focus of his advertisements — and, thanks to strong fundraising due in no small part to his last name, he hit the television airwaves much earlier than candidates for lower-level statewide offices in Indiana typically do.

“The Republican Party has had a monopoly on control of state government here in Indiana, and the natural product of little to no competition is unreasonable results,” Bayh told CNN days after the election.

Exit polls revealed the wisdom of Bayh’s decision.CNN Voter Pollsfound that voters nationally in 2026 ranked corruption as the single most important issue to their votes — slightly ahead of the cost of living.

Bayh said he thought the message resonated “because it cuts across party lines. It cuts across ideology.”

It’s also what voters raised to him most frequently on the campaign trail — and what Bayh said personally incensed him, as he looked around the country.

He has promised an independent audit of the secretary of state’s office. But he also said he sees his role as “acting as an independent voice in the Statehouse to call out some areas where I think our state government has gone wrong that are not within the confines of this office.”

Around Indiana, one question that older Democrats often ask is whether Beau Bayh, whose full name is Birch Evans Bayh IV, inherited his politics from Birch or Evan.

Birch, a three-term senator, was a folksy, backslapping lover of retail politics who was nevertheless a sophisticated progressive reformer in Washington. He authored Title IX and was a chief architect of the 25th and 26th amendments to the Constitution and the Equal Rights Amendment. Time Magazine in 1975 described his style as “both country ham and hard ball — take your pick.”

Evan, a two-term governor and two-term senator, was much more reserved and disciplined. He also cut a reputation as more moderate than his father — which irritated some liberals, but made him a political force. He won reelection to the Senate in 2004 with 62% of the vote even as President George W. Bush won 60% in Indiana — showing the kind of political resilience Birch couldn’t when he was wiped out by Ronald Reagan’s 1980 wave. Unlike Birch, though, he left the Senate without major legislation bearing his name, and after retiring in 2010, he fell short in an attempted political comeback when he ran again for his old seat in 2016.

Birch ran for president in 1976 but dropped out after weak showings in early states; Evan launched an exploratory committee in 2008 but closed it weeks later.

Like Beau, both were young when they entered politics. Their time in elected office also ended early — Birch’s at 52; Evan’s at 56.

In the lead-up to the election, Republicans sought to brand Bayh as a phony riding the coattails of his family name. Lana Keesling, who was chairwoman of the Indiana Republican Party until her resignation last week, called Bayh “a far-left political nepo baby.” In ads, Engling said Bayh “thinks this seat is his birthright.”

It’s too soon to tell how Beau Bayh sees his position within the Democratic Party.

“He doesn’t have to be captive to some of the categories and labels that have defined a previous generation of politics,” Buttigieg said. “It’s for him to work out what makes sense. But there are seasons where being pragmatic means being bold. And we’ll see what that season means for someone like Beau.”

Beshear, whose father, Steve Beshear, was also governor of Kentucky, said Bayh doesn’t have a chip on his shoulder that drives him to break from his family’s legacy.

Beau Bayh, Beshear said, “is self-confident enough to ask his dad at different times about things.”

“Having a father that was governor meant that I didn’t step on all the same land mines,” Beshear said. “I had advice in certain instances that helped me be a better governor. That doesn’t mean I haven’t made my own path.”

However, when it comes to how he stacks up to members of his own political family, what many took as a hint came at the end of his run for secretary of state. His final television commercial featured the exact same jingle his grandfather blanketed Indiana airwaves with in 1962 to teach Hoosiers how to pronounce his last name (it’s “buy”).

Stylistically, most Hoosier Democrats compare Beau to Birch. Beau agreed — but also pointed to his mother, Susan Bayh, who died of glioblastoma in 2021.

He said she and Evan Bayh made a “perfect political team” because while Evan was reserved and thoughtful, Susan “was very outgoing and energetic, and would talk to anybody.”

Speaking with CNN just before Election Day, Bayh also identified another Midwestern politician he admired: Rob Sand, the Iowa governor-elect.

Sand, like Bayh, has sought to cut an image as impervious to partisan politics. Sand opened town halls in Iowa by asking members of each political affiliation — Republican, Democratic and independent — to applaud the others for being there, and by leading the crowd in singing the first verse of “America the Beautiful.”

It’s the same philosophy Bayh said he brings to the campaign trail.

“I will just go anywhere. I’ll talk to anyone. I’ll field public questions — not all of which are easy, but I’m going to try and listen to people and empathize with them, even if we don’t agree.”

He added: “And that’s not just fielding questions at a town hall, but that’s looking at people in the eye and talking to them one on one and showing them that I truly care.”
